A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REPPO. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections. Internal setting inconsistencies limit particular interpretations but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original toy-gradient experiments, DMC and ManiSkill evaluations, architectural and memory ablations, and discrete REPPO results on Atari-10.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds gradient-path comparisons, KL and data-scaling analyses, and REPPO evaluations on IsaacLab.

M1.justification: v4 revises the discrete KL penalty to average under the behavior policy (v3 Equation 19; v4 Equation 15) and aligns the formal constraint and tuning direction with the forward KL already used by v3's clipped loss. These are limited revisions to the reported loss specification; the core training loop and architecture persist. Implementation changes are not established.

E1.justification: Appendix E.3 adds four IsaacLab H1/G1 velocity-tracking environments spanning flat and rough terrain, extending simulator and terrain coverage within locomotion. The original 23 DMC tasks, eight ManiSkill environments, Atari-10 games, and toy objective are retained.

E2.justification: SAC (Brax, 5M) joins the wall-clock comparison in v4 Figure 7; v3 Figure 6 compared PPO implementations only. The new toy comparison also evaluates importance-sampled REINFORCE and PPO-style clipped importance sampling. Existing principal benchmark comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v4 adds an eight-step resampling-versus-reuse toy protocol, a four-configuration rollout/minibatch scaling study for PPO and REPPO, and IsaacLab evaluation up to 250 million steps with a KL target of 0.01 rather than the default 0.1. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Exact scaling budgets remain ambiguous: Figure 12a labels 1024 environments times 32 steps as a 65k buffer. Default Table 2 settings otherwise remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds a reverse-KL ablation, quantifies the unclipped alternative already discussed in v3, and expands buffer analysis to compare PPO and REPPO across four configurations. Figure 3b additionally examines variance from importance sampling and clipping through repeated gradient paths. These extend the questions tested beyond v3's retained component-removal and two-buffer-size analyses.

E5.justification: Section 2.2 newly reports 100 different eight-step trajectories for the gradient-path comparison. Main benchmark reporting still specifies 20 REPPO and PPO seeds, five FastTD3 seeds, and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. No increase in those benchmark run counts is documented.

E6.justification: v4 adds IsaacLab, SAC runtime, gradient-path, KL-ablation, and data-scaling results. It also revises ManiSkill aggregates: the plotted 50M-step PPO mean changes from approximately 0.82 to 0.79 (v3 Figure 4b; v4 Figure 5b). The memory comparison changes estimates and relabels the smaller REPPO buffer from 32k to 65k, preventing an unambiguous same-setting comparison. Main DMC results and Atari Table 1 are retained.

T1.justification: v4 changes the n-step return's summation limits and discount powers (v3 Equation 7; v4 Equation 5), replaces the constrained objective's maximum-entropy return with expected Q (v3 Equation 10; v4 Equation 8), and removes the explicit discounted-occupancy formula. These are localized mathematical-specification revisions; neither version provides a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that on-policy Q learning enables effective pathwise updates, that joint entropy/KL control stabilizes learning, and that REPPO improves performance and reliability over PPO with low memory requirements. v4 foregrounds Q-based action resampling and removal of importance sampling, but these benefits were already claimed in v3.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands the mechanism discussion: importance sampling amplifies variance despite clipping, forward KL better complements entropy maximization for the chosen policies, and dataset scaling affects REPPO and PPO differently. Appendix E.2 adds a KL-imposed limit on continued improvement from fixed data. The SAC discussion also qualifies performance comparisons by computational cost, while IsaacLab introduces a boundary to default-hyperparameter transfer.

D1.justification: v4 reports an RSL-RL implementation, changes the code-access location from cvoelcker/reppo to reppo-rl, and newly explains preparation of the tuned 50M-step PPO baseline. It supplies scaling configurations and the IsaacLab KL setting. Conversely, v3 Figure 6's explicit L40s hardware disclosure disappears. The existing architecture and default hyperparameter documentation largely persist.

R1.justification: Most related work is retained in Appendix A. Limited additions include Neumann and Sokota on KL direction, Palenicek on cross-entropy optimization, Nauman's categorical value-function work, and IsaacLab/RSL-RL references. v4 also explicitly positions its on-policy value updates as closer to SARSA than Q-learning.

P1.justification: v4 substantially reorganizes the exposition: related work moves to Appendix A, pseudocode to Appendix F, and HL-Gauss and auxiliary-task formulations to Appendix D. The abstract, introduction, background, and gradient-variance discussion are rewritten or condensed. Author formatting, equal-contribution information, acknowledgments, and the publication header also change.

P2.justification: v4 adds an algorithm-overview figure, expands the toy illustration into a multipart figure, extends the runtime and KL-ablation plots, and rebuilds the memory display as Figure 12 with a configuration table and scaling panel. It adds four IsaacLab learning curves and relocates several retained displays. The ManiSkill long-horizon PPO label changes from 200M to 100M, matching the retained caption.

improvement.justification: v4 provides more direct evidence for the choice of KL direction and the variance introduced by importance sampling, questions v3 supported less directly. IsaacLab also tests transfer to additional locomotion settings. These gains outweigh localized drawbacks, particularly inconsistent buffer sizes in Figure 12a and removal of the L40s runtime-hardware disclosure, but constitute a limited improvement over v3's already extensive evaluation.
